Am I required to carry it?

Only if your home is in a high-risk zone (A or V) and your mortgage is from a federally regulated lender, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Check your zone on FEMA's flood map.

70.0% of Florida's NFIP policies are in high-risk zones (not 70.0% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

How much does it cost here?

Typically about $983 a year ($82 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $661 and $1,394. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

The bar is the middle half of policies, from 759,007 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price; a brand-new policy is priced at full risk.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Buy it now: most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there's no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, or change coverage at renewal; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. If FEMA aid pays to repair a home in a high-risk zone, you must buy and keep flood insurance on it, or you cannot get that aid again after a later flood. Past aid paid here is in “Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?” below.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 448,618 NFIP flood claims and $19.3 billion in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2024, 2022 and 2004.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2024 ($7,890,762,813), 2022 ($4,941,023,184), 2004 ($1,246,778,017). Total paid $19,301,860,211: net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 448,618 claims since 1978 against 1,795,894 policies in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

Most do: 69.9% of claims here paid something. The average paid claim was $61,756.

  • Average paid claim$61,756
  • Closed with no payment30.1%
  • Claims that paid313,446

FEMA lists reasons a claim closes without payment, such as damage below the deductible, no flood as the policy defines it, or seepage and drain backup the policy does not cover. The average is over claims that paid something and includes Increased Cost of Compliance payments (help to elevate or rebuild to code), which the yearly totals above leave out. Dollars are as paid at the time, not adjusted for inflation; a single home can file across several floods over the years.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

NFIP covers up to $250,000 on the building and $100,000 on contents, which is a separate policy. Rebuilding cost is the replacement-cost figure on each single-family primary-home policy record.

Why do sites quote different averages for Florida?

Because they measure different things. From the same FEMA records, the typical single-family home pays $983 a year, but the average across every policy type is $1,868.

MeasureAmountWhat it counts
Median cost, single-family homes$983premium plus fees; the middle policy
Average (mean) cost, single-family homes$1,377pulled up by a few expensive policies
Median premium only, single-family homes$772before the federal fee, reserve fund and surcharge
Average premium only, single-family homes$1,106the figure many sites quote
Median cost, every policy type$1,083adds condos, rentals and businesses
Average cost, every policy type$1,868

Published averages rarely say which of these they are, or which year. All six here come from the NFIP policies in force on July 31, 2026.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

49.8% of policies here pay less than FEMA's full-risk price, so their bills are rising toward it. Median premium $772, full-risk $933 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$772
  • Median full-risk premium$933
  • Pay below full-risk49.8% of 759,006

Yearly cap: Those prices step up toward full-risk each year, limited by the yearly cap. By law a primary home's premium cannot rise more than 18% a year; some policies, such as second homes and businesses, can rise up to 25%. The cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. Bills already at full risk still change with FEMA's yearly rate updates.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How often do the same homes flood here?

Yes: FEMA's disaster-aid records hold 62,664 damage records from homes here that flooded more than once; 1,927 records are from homes on FEMA's severe repetitive loss list.

  • Repeat-flood damage records62,664
  • Records from homes on the severe repetitive loss list1,927

One home appears once for each declared disaster that damaged it, so this counts damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes (FEMA says these records cannot be totaled by property). Disaster-aid records since 2002, separate from NFIP insurance claims.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Individual Assistance Multiple-Loss Flood Properties. Data: FEMA's current multiple-loss list; retrieved October 26, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $4.2 billion for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $1,040 per registration, against an average paid flood-insurance claim of $61,756.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Hurricane aid includes wind damage. COVID, fire, ice-storm and tornado aid are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners); FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Are these counts complete?

Every record FEMA's download lists was received and counted. FEMA also publishes a separate official policy count, which we have not yet compared for Florida.

In-force count: 1,795,894 policy units (from 1,130,989 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). Count reconciliation (not a snapshot proof): policies: 1,130,989 of 1,130,989 fetched; claims: 448,618 of 448,618 fetched.

What this data cannot tell you

  • Your own premium — it depends on elevation, coverage and deductible. We show where existing policies fall.
  • Private (non-NFIP) flood insurance prices.
  • Your address's exact flood zone — use FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.
  • Why any one premium changes — we show the gap to full-risk, not the cause.
  • A year-over-year premium trend — the in-force snapshot holds only current-term policies, so a like-for-like multi-year index isn't possible from this data. A per-effective-year median is shown only where several years of policies exist.

The federal datasets behind this page

Every figure comes from a public U.S. federal dataset; estimates are labeled where they appear. This page joins 8 of them for Florida. The newest of these downloads was October 26, 2026.
